title: Why Uber cut the world into hexagons
subtitle: From map shapes to one number per place

scenes.title: A city as a ride app sees it
scenes.narration: Picture a busy city the way a ride app sees it. Every driver and every rider is a dot, and the city is cut into districts.

steps.say: The districts come from old maps, like postcodes. Their borders are jagged, and no two are the same size.
Each dot is a pair of numbers, a latitude and a longitude, and it moves every few seconds.
This car sits right on the border between two of them. Cross the street, and it lands in the other one, with a different price.
To learn if a point is inside Old Town, draw a line out from it and count how often it crosses Old Town's outline. It crosses once, an odd number, so the car is inside.

steps.callout: each check walks every border edge
steps.say: The database does this for every car. Each check walks every corner of every border it tests.
With thousands of cars asking every few seconds, the query falls behind and times out.

scenes.title: Three shapes that tile a flat map
scenes.narration: Only three regular shapes cover a flat map with no gaps: triangles, squares and hexagons. Look at how far away each cell's neighbours are.

steps.say: A triangle touches twelve others, at three different distances. That makes "nearby" messy.
A square has four neighbours along its sides, all at the same distance, call it d.
But the four corner neighbours are about one point four times as far. Forty one percent farther, yet they still count as next door.
A hexagon has six neighbours, and every one is exactly the same distance away. No corner problem, so spreading things out to nearby cells stays even.

scenes.title: From a ball to flat triangles
scenes.narration: The earth is a ball, and hexagons alone can't cover a ball. So H3 starts with a twenty sided shape inside it.

steps.say: Put a shape made of twenty triangles inside the ball, touching it at its corners.
Cut it open and lay it flat. Each triangle becomes a flat map of its own patch of the earth, and hexagons tile each one.
There's a catch at the twelve corners, where five triangles meet. A rule about closed shapes says some cells must have five sides, and here it's exactly twelve.
So every level has twelve pentagons. H3 turns the shape so all twelve land in the ocean, where nobody calls a car.

scenes.title: Each cell holds seven smaller ones
scenes.narration: Here is one big hexagon. H3 fills it with smaller hexagons, then fills each of those again.

steps.say: Start with one big cell.
Seven smaller cells sit inside it: one in the middle and six around it.
Seven hexagons only make a big hexagon shape when they're turned, so each level sits turned about nineteen degrees from the one above.
Do it again, and each of the seven holds seven more. Forty nine.
The fit isn't perfect. The small cells poke out past the big one's edge a little, and that's fine for counting cars.
H3 repeats this sixteen times, from level zero to level fifteen.

scenes.title: H3 levels Uber leans on
scenes.narration: Each level is about seven times smaller in area than the one above. Uber picks the level that fits the job.

steps.say: The biggest level has a hundred and twenty two cells for the whole planet. The smallest is under one square metre.
Matching happens at level nine, where a cell is about two hundred metres across an edge. That's about a city block.
Surge pricing looks at levels seven and eight, where many blocks are counted together.
To go from a level nine cell to the level seven cell that holds it, you don't touch the map. You just change a few bits in its name.

scenes.title: A cell's name is one number
scenes.narration: Every H3 cell has a name that fits in one 64 bit number. This one names a cell in downtown San Francisco, at level eight.

steps.callout: mode 1 = this number names a cell
steps.say: The first bits are housekeeping. The mode is one, which says this number names a cell.
Four bits hold the level. Here it's eight.
Seven bits say which of the hundred and twenty two biggest cells it sits in. Here it's number twenty.
Then come fifteen digits of three bits, each from zero to six. Each digit says which of the seven smaller cells to step into, one step at a time. This cell takes eight steps, so it uses eight digits.
Levels this cell doesn't reach hold a seven, all three bits on, which means not used.
To get the parent one level up, set the level to seven and mark the eighth digit not used. A few bit changes, and no map lookup.

scenes.title: Searching ring by ring
scenes.narration: A rider asks for a car. Instead of measuring the distance to every car in the city, the app looks at cells around the rider.
scenes.callout: old way: √(dx² + dy²) for every car

steps.say: The rider is in this cell. Its name is one number.
First, look up the six cells that touch it. Each is one lookup in a table of cars by cell. No cars there.

steps.callout: ring 2: 12 more cells, 19 in all, 3 cars
steps.say: Widen by one ring. That's twelve more cells, nineteen in all, and three cars.

steps.callout: only 3 cars go to the routing engine
steps.say: Only those three cars go to the routing engine, which works out real driving times on real roads.
Cars farther out are never even looked at.

scenes.title: Before and after H3
scenes.narration: Here is what the switch bought Uber. They released H3 as open source in 2018.

rows.label: Which area is a car in?
cells: Walk every edge of a border

steps.say: Finding a car's area went from checking border edges to reading a number.
Pricing areas went from jagged districts to even hexagons.
A place went from two sixty four bit numbers to one, a whole number you can group by and compare.
And rolling small cells up into bigger ones went from merging shapes to changing a few bits.
